1:
Gill fixes the occasion: the order comes after the numbering, as the congregation was about to set forward, and governs both how they camped and how they marched. Calvin reads the whole arrangement as a device against contention, and names the quarrels it forestalled. Reuben's family would have found it grievous to resign the firstborn's dignity for the lowest place; the sons of the two handmaids would not have thought it just that Leah's and Rachel's children should always outrank them; each tribe would have claimed precedence in proportion to its numbers; and the division of Joseph into two required divine authority, since Manasseh, superior by the law of nature, would never otherwise have consented to follow Ephraim. Wesley works the same problem from kinship rather than grievance, and here he is not repeating Henry but reasoning on his own: Judah, Issachar and Zebulun were the three youngest sons of Leah, so the younger two would not grudge to serve under their elder brother; Gad, a son of Leah's handmaid, is fitly added to Reuben in Levi's room; the third standard gathers all the posterity of Rachel; and Dan, eldest son of Bilhah, leads the rest. Keil notes the effect of putting Judah first, that his standard marched out at the head as champion of his brethren, as Jacob's blessing had said of him.

On what the standards looked like the sources are frank that nobody knows. Henry says plainly it is uncertain, and lays out three conjectures without choosing between them: that each standard matched the colour of the stone bearing that tribe's name in the high priest's ephod, and that this was the only difference; that each bore arms drawn from Jacob's blessing, a lion for Judah, a serpent for Dan, a hind for Naphtali, a wolf for Benjamin; or that the four principal standards were lion, man, ox and eagle, which would make Ezekiel's vision allude to them. Wesley grants four great ensigns distinguished by colours or figures, with further particular ensigns for the fathers' houses under them. Clarke reproduces the Talmudists' full list, down to an ass for Issachar, a ship for Zebulun and a handful of corn for Asher, then does what none of the others attempt: he prints an entire reconstructed plan of the camp, with square-cubit allotments tribe by tribe and a total of a little more than twelve square miles. Having spread all of it before the reader he withdraws its authority himself. The text says which tribes held which quarter and no more; how they were arranged individually cannot be pretended to, and to claim minute exactness there would be absurd.

The tabernacle in the midst draws the fullest treatment. Henry compares it to a general's pavilion at the centre of an army, and gets two things from the position: it was equally a comfort to all of them, since they had God in the heart of the camp, and equally their charge, since no invader could reach it without breaking through the thickest of their squadrons. He supposes the tent doors were made to open toward it on every side. Both he and Wesley must then account for the qualification that they pitched far off. Henry takes it as reverence, that the sanctuary should not seem crowded and thrust up among them, and adds the blunter reason, lest too much familiarity breed contempt; Wesley adds caution to reverence, that nearness might tempt them to approach what was not theirs to approach, and both put the distance at two thousand cubits. Clarke sets the same arrangement out as three camps, of the Lord, of the Levites and of the people, answering to the holy of holies, the holy place and the outer court. Henry alone presses the contrast: we are not ordered as they were to pitch afar off, but invited to draw near and come boldly.
3:
Henry puts the reason for divine appointment in the negative, by asking who else could have done it. Left to settle precedence among themselves the tribes would have quarrelled, as the disciples did over which should be greatest, since every one of them had a pretence to be first or at least not to be last; and had Moses decided it they would have charged him with partiality. So God does it, being himself the fountain and judge of honour, and in his appointment all must acquiesce. Henry then turns the point on the reader: where our place is providentially fixed we should be as satisfied as if a voice out of the tabernacle had assigned it, and where it is left to our own choice we have our Saviour's rules, not to sit down in the highest room, and that whoever will be chief must be servant. He takes the captains the same way. That we are all children of one Adam does not abolish distinctions of place and honour, since even among the children of the same Abraham and the same Jacob God himself appointed that one should be captain over the rest; there are powers ordained of God to whom honour and fear are due.

The princes' names give Henry his one piece of historical inference, and it is the most interesting thing he does here. Most of these men carry God's name at one end or other of their own, and he runs through them: Nethaneel, the gift of God; Eliab, my God a Father; Elizur, my God a rock; Shelumiel, God my peace; Eliasaph, God has added; Elishama, my God has heard; Gamaliel, God my reward; Pagiel, God has met me. From that he draws a conclusion about the generation that named them. The Israelites in Egypt had not forgotten the name of their God; when other memorials failed them they preserved the remembrance of it in the names of their children, and comforted themselves with it in their affliction. Gill works at a smaller scale in the same verses, noting from Jarchi that the east is called Kedem, what is before, as the west is called what is behind, and adding an observation of Aben Ezra's that between the numbering and the setting forward twenty days passed in which not one of those counted died, so that the totals repeated here still stood exactly as taken. Keil glosses the formula that carries them, reading the host and those that were numbered of them as the army reckoned according to its mustered men.

On why Judah led, Henry and Wesley give the same answer in nearly the same words, Wesley condensing Henry as he has done throughout: not only because the tribe was the most numerous, but chiefly because Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, was to descend from it, and from the loins of Nahshon, the man here named its chief captain. Henry presses further than Wesley follows him. Nahshon is reckoned among the ancestors of Christ, so that when he went before the camp Christ in effect went before them as their leader; and Judah, though not the firstborn, was the first of Jacob's sons to be blessed, Reuben and Simeon and Levi having been censured by their dying father, which Henry turns into a lesson for children on valuing a godly parent's smiles and dreading his frowns. Gill declines the theology and corrects the picture instead. The three tribes did not stand in file, Judah first and the others behind in order; Judah lay between them, with Issachar behind and Zebulun before, one on each side of the standard, and being Leah's youngest sons and Judah's own brothers they pitched under their elder brother without reluctance.
10:
Gill supplies for the southern camp what none of the others attempt, a description of the flags themselves out of the Jewish writers, tribe by tribe. Reuben's stone was the sardius, his flag coloured red with mandrakes figured on it; Simeon's the topaz, his flag green, with Shechem figured on it; Gad's the agate, his flag neither black nor white but mixed, with a camp or host figured on it in allusion to what was said of him. He also gives the orientation from Aben Ezra, that the south is the right hand, so that this was the right wing of the whole army, and he keeps host and camp carefully distinct, the host of Reuben being only a part of the camp that bore his name and Elizur the captain of that host rather than of the three tribes. Keil states the same grouping in flatter terms and adds the descent that explains it: Simeon and Gad, sprung from Leah and from Leah's maid Zilpah, were associated with Reuben's standard and subordinated to it.

On why these three could be put together without resentment Gill argues from the family history at each step. Simeon pitches under Reuben's standard because the two were brothers by the mother's side as well as the father's, so they might well be thought to agree; and because Reuben was not merely the elder of the two but the eldest of all Jacob's sons, Simeon would not grudge to pitch under him. Gad stands on the opposite side of the standard, which fixes the arrangement on the ground, Reuben before and Simeon behind. Gad's own position Gill grounds in his birth twice over: as the eldest son of Leah's handmaid Zilpah he is fitly placed under Leah's firstborn, and as the son of a handmaid he could not object to his situation. The reasoning is worth marking because it is doing the same work Calvin's does at the head of the chapter, only from the other end. Calvin argues that the arrangement forestalled quarrels; Gill shows, tribe by tribe, why in these particular pairings no quarrel could arise.

The tabernacle setting forward in the midst gets two different kinds of attention. Gill stays with measurement and emblem: the camp of the Levites reached four miles, according to the Targum of Jonathan, the same extent as Judah's; Levi's stone was the carbuncle, and his flag was coloured in three parts, white, black and red, with the Urim and Thummim figured on it. Wesley raises the question the phrase invites and answers it against the obvious reading. In the midst is not to be understood strictly but largely, since on the march the tribe was divided, part of it going next after Judah and only the other part exactly in the centre of the camp. Keil, for his part, flags a difficulty in the text rather than in the arrangement, noting that the name given here as the father of the captain of Gad does not agree with the form used of the same man in the first chapter and again in the seventh; the block in which he says so is cut off before he settles which of the two forms he takes to be the error.
18:
The western camp brought the sharpest inversion of birth order in the chapter, and Wesley disposes of it in a single clause: Ephraim is preferred before his brother according to the prophecy Jacob made when he crossed his hands over Joseph's sons. Gill spends longer showing why nobody in that camp had grounds to complain. Manasseh, though the elder, was given no standard and was directed to pitch by his younger brother's; but since this agreed with Jacob's prophecy it could not well be objected to. Benjamin was Joseph's own younger brother, and being placed under the standard of a son of Joseph who stood in his father's room, he could not be offended either. And all three were Rachel's descendants, so they might well be thought to agree together and be content with their situation. Keil states the same fact without the reasoning, treating the western standard simply as the whole of Rachel's posterity, 108,100 men, forming the third division of the army and going forward in the third rank.

Gill continues his catalogue of the flags here, and the details he reports are more particular than for any other camp. Joseph's stone was the onyx or sardonyx, and his flag was coloured very black, with Egypt figured on it for the two princes because they were born there. Ephraim's flag carried an ox and Manasseh's a unicorn, both drawn from the same blessing of Moses. Benjamin's stone was the jasper, his flag coloured like twelve colours, and a wolf figured on it, from what Jacob had said of him. Gill also fixes the arrangement on the ground as he did in the south: Benjamin pitched under Ephraim's standard on the side opposite Manasseh, so that one was before and the other behind with the standard between them, and the whole camp extended four miles, the same figure the Targum of Jonathan gives for Judah and for Levi.

On the totals Gill makes the observation that gives this camp its character. The numbered men of Ephraim's camp were a hundred and eight thousand and a hundred, which he notes was the smallest of all four camps, nearly eighty thousand fewer than Judah's in the east. He keeps host and camp distinct here as elsewhere, so that the separate numbers of Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin are the hosts and the larger figure is the camp they compose between them. Keil gives the same total and the same place in the order of march and supplies nothing further. The result is that the tribe raised over its elder brother by prophecy heads the weakest of the four divisions, and that both writers record the precedence and the weakness without remark, Gill having already settled the precedence on Jacob's word rather than on any strength in Ephraim.
25:
Gill finishes his survey of the flags with the northern camp, which he places to the left of the tabernacle as the left wing of the grand army, its extent again four miles by the Targum of Jonathan. Dan's stone was the ligure, his flag coloured like a sapphire with a serpent figured on it; Asher's the tarshish or beryl, his flag coloured like the precious stone with which women adorn themselves, with an olive tree on it; Naphtali's the amethyst, his flag coloured like clear wine whose redness is not strong, with a hind on it. On why a son of a handmaid should have a standard at all Gill gives three reasons together: Dan was the firstborn of the handmaids' sons, his tribe was warlike, and it was very numerous. The two placed with him could not object, being sons of handmaids themselves, Naphtali his younger brother by the mother's side as well as the father's and Asher the second son of Zilpah, so that the eldest of that group led the rest.

Wesley alone explains why this camp was posted where it was, and does it in tactical terms rather than genealogical. Dan's was the strongest camp after Judah's, and therefore it came in the rear as Judah marched in the front, so that the tabernacle would be best guarded at the point of greatest danger. Gill supplies the figure that supports him, a hundred and fifty-seven thousand six hundred, the largest camp next to Judah's. Keil, characteristically, takes the same verse as a question about words. The text says they shall go hindmost with their standards, and he observes that the phrase according to their standards is equivalent to the phrase according to their hosts used of the three earlier camps, meaning in each case the hosts of which the camp consisted. So on his reading the closing formula for Dan is not a different kind of statement from the others but the same one worded differently.

The summary verses draw the sharpest divergence in method of the whole chapter. Gill treats them as narrative and fills in what obedience actually consisted of: they formed themselves into camps, so many tribes to a camp, appointed a captain over each tribe, erected a standard to each camp, pitched every man by the standard he belonged to, and marched in that order, families under tribes and lesser houses under families, as they did on the twentieth day of that month. He also notes that the numbering was taken by Moses and Aaron with the twelve princes who are now made captains, and that the Levites were counted separately because they were a camp of themselves. Keil reads the same verse as a literary matter. Giving the total of six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty apart from the Levites, he calls the closing statement that the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded an anticipatory notice of what was carried out later, of the same kind as the closing remarks in Exodus about the passover and the setting up of the tabernacle.
